newsitem.title: ANGOLA: SOUTHERN AFRICAN LEADERS ARRIVE FOR ANGOLAN SUMMIT.
newsitem.headline: SOUTHERN AFRICAN LEADERS ARRIVE FOR ANGOLAN SUMMIT.

text.p: Southern African heads of state began arriving in the Angolan capital Luanda on Tuesday night ahead of a leaders' summit to boost the country's slow-moving peace process.
Botswana's President Ketumile Masire was the first head of state for the Southern African Development Community (SADC) group of countries to arrive at Luanda's international airport.
He was followed by the presidents of Mozambique, Namibia, Zambia and Zimbabwe. Delegates from Mauritius, Swaziland and Lesotho were due to arrive later.
South African President Nelson Mandela, the head of SADC, is due in Luanda early on Wednesday before the start of the one-day summit.
It is the first meeting of its kind in Angola by southern African leaders who are keen to see Angola's fragile two-year peace completed.
The Angolan government and former rebel UNITA movement signed a peace accord in neighbouring Zambia in 1994 to end two decades of fighting and Africa's longest war.

Angolan President Jose Eduardo dos Santos, government ministers and the United Nations chief peace negotiator to Angola, Alioune Blondin Beye, greeted foreign guests, who arrived at half-hour intervals from 4 p.m.
Zimbabwe's President Robert Mugabe told reporters the leaders would be briefed by Dos Santos later on the peace process.

"We of SADC would want to see the process of peace in Angola proceed much more rapidly than it has been and so our expectation is that we will be briefed first by President dos Santos and others on how the peace process is progressing or not progressing, and why.
"We will look at it and together we will try and find a way of accelerating the process, so there is greater peace and stability in Angola," Mugabe said.
Asked if the summit would have the same impetus if UNITA leader Jonas Savimbi did not attend the meeting, Mugabe replied:
"We will examine all that. If he is not here today it does not mean he won't be here tomorrow, so we will have to be patient. Peace demands a great amount of patience if it is to be realised at all."
Mugabe added he hoped Savimbi would attend the meeting.
There was no word if the 62-year-old Savimbi, notoriously careful of his physical safety, would accept an invitation by SADC to attend the meeting.
A UNITA official in Luanda told Reuters he doubted Savimbi would arrive. "I doubt very much that Dr Savimbi will come, but then again he is a man of many surprises."
Savimbi's chief constitutional negotiator Abel Chivukuvuku said the UNITA leader wanted a personal invitation to the summit by dos Santos.

But a senior U.N. official told Reuters on Tuesday that Beye had delivered a letter from dos Santos and another from the U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros Ghali last week urging him to attend the meeting.

The Angolan government tightly secured Luanda's streets ahead of the arrival of the heads of state. Armed soldiers were placed at every corner on the major routes to hotels where guests had been booked in.
The police headquarters said in a statement broadcast on state radio earlier in the day that hawkers were prohibited from selling near hotels and closed taxi ranks near the airport.
A major operation was also implemented on Tuesday to clean the city's streets and sidewalks for the meeting.
The 12-nation SADC groups Mauritius, Angola, Lesotho, Swaziland, Zambia, Zimbabwe, Namibia, Mozambique, Tanzania, Malawi, Botswana and South Africa.
